name: Wolfram Mathematica
description: Wolfram Mathematica is an integrated technical computing system built on the Wolfram Language, a symbolic, term-rewriting programming language in which everything is an expression. A single environment covers exact and arbitrary-precision arithmetic, symbolic algebra, calculus, equation solving, linear algebra, discrete mathematics, probability and statistics, optimization, differential equations, visualization, string and text processing, units and dates, image and signal processing, graphs and networks, machine learning, and a large curated knowledge base of real-world data. Programs are written in a mixture of functional, rule-based, list-oriented and procedural styles, and the same code runs interactively in notebooks, headless from the command line through wolframscript, inside other languages via the Wolfram Client Library, or deployed to the Wolfram Cloud as web APIs and forms. This catalog covers the core language and the symbolic and numeric mathematics functionality that ships with every copy of Mathematica; no add-on packages are required.

automation.summary: Mathematica is automated in five main ways. (1) wolframscript, the command-line front end to a local or cloud Wolfram kernel: `wolframscript -code "expr"` evaluates an expression and prints the result, `wolframscript -file script.wl` runs a package file, and `wolframscript -script script.wls` runs a script with `$ScriptCommandLine` populated so it behaves like a normal Unix/Windows command. (2) The legacy kernel executables `math`/`wolfram`, which read Wolfram Language input from stdin or a file (`wolfram -script file.wl`, `math -noprompt -run "..."`). (3) The Wolfram Client Library for Python (`pip install wolframclient`), which starts or attaches to a kernel from Python, evaluates Wolfram Language expressions and converts results to native Python objects; the same wire protocol (WSTP/MathLink) underlies the C, Java (J/Link) and .NET (.NET/Link) interfaces. (4) Cloud deployment: `CloudDeploy` combined with `APIFunction`, `FormFunction` or `Delayed` publishes a Wolfram Language function as an HTTP endpoint or web form that any client can call. (5) In the other direction, `ExternalEvaluate`, `RunProcess`, `LibraryFunctionLoad`, `URLRead` and `ServiceExecute` let Wolfram Language code drive Python, shell commands, native shared libraries, REST services and external APIs. Headless batch work typically writes a `.wls` script, runs it with wolframscript, and exchanges data through `Export`/`Import` (JSON, CSV, MX, WXF) or through stdout.

cli.description: Evaluate one Wolfram Language expression in a fresh kernel and print the result in InputForm to stdout, then exit. The quickest way to call Mathematica from a shell, Makefile or another program. Use `-format` (e.g. `-format JSON`, `-format Text`, `-format TeX`) to control how the result is serialized.

Read and evaluate a Wolfram Language package/source file line by line, printing whatever the file prints, then exit. Nothing is echoed unless the file calls `Print`, `Echo` or `Export`, so this is the normal form for batch jobs that write their results to disk.

Run a `.wls` script file with command-line arguments available in `$ScriptCommandLine`. In this mode `Print` output goes to stdout, the kernel does not print `In[]`/`Out[]` labels, and `Exit[n]` sets the process exit code, so the script behaves like any other CLI tool. On Unix a `#!/usr/bin/env wolframscript` shebang plus the executable bit makes the file directly runnable.

Choose the output serialization with `-format` (Text, InputForm, JSON, TeX, Image, PNG, ...) and redirect it to a file with `-o`/`-output`. Combine with `-format JSON` when the caller is a script that must parse the answer.

Apply a Wolfram Language function directly to command-line arguments without writing a script. `-args` supplies the arguments as strings; add `-signature` to declare `Interpreter` types so the strings are parsed into numbers, dates or quantities first.

Run the code in the Wolfram Cloud rather than on a local kernel, so no local licence or installation is needed. `-cloud <base>` selects an alternate cloud; `-authenticate` stores credentials for later non-interactive runs; `-api <uuid_or_url>` calls a deployed `APIFunction`.

Run a file with the kernel executable itself (`wolfram` on all platforms, also `WolframKernel`). Equivalent to `wolframscript -script` for most purposes and available on systems where the wolframscript wrapper is not on the PATH.

Legacy text-mode kernel invocation. `-noprompt` suppresses the `In[]`/`Out[]` prompts, `-initfile` evaluates a file before reading input, and Wolfram Language statements are piped in on stdin; finish the input with `Quit[]` so the kernel exits. `math` is the historical name of the kernel launcher on Unix; `wolfram` is the modern equivalent.

Print the value of every expression in the file, not just the last one. `-print` (or `-print all`) is useful when converting an interactive notebook session into a batch script and you want each result echoed.

apis.name: Wolfram Client Library for Python
apis.description: The official Python package (`pip install wolframclient`) starts a local kernel with `WolframLanguageSession` (or connects to the cloud with `WolframCloudSession`) and evaluates Wolfram Language code from Python. `wl` and `wlexpr` build expressions: `wl.Total([1,2,3])` constructs symbolic expressions from Python objects, while `wlexpr("...")` parses Wolfram Language source. Results are converted to native Python types automatically, and `session.function(...)` turns a Wolfram function into a callable Python object.
apis.example:
from wolframclient.evaluation import WolframLanguageSession
from wolframclient.language import wl, wlexpr

session = WolframLanguageSession()
print(session.evaluate(wlexpr('Integrate[Sin[x]^2, {x, 0, Pi}]')))
print(session.evaluate(wl.Total([1, 2, 3, 4])))

factor = session.function(wlexpr('FactorInteger'))
print(factor(2**64 + 1))

session.terminate()

apis.name: Wolfram Language (scripts and packages)
apis.description: The primary automation surface is the language itself. A `.wls` script is executed top to bottom by wolframscript; a `.wl`/`.m` package uses `BeginPackage`/`EndPackage` to declare a public context and is loaded with `Get` or `Needs`. Definitions are ordinary rewrite rules attached to symbols, and `Options`/`OptionsPattern` give functions named options exactly like built-ins.

apis.name: WSTP / MathLink
apis.description: Wolfram Symbolic Transfer Protocol is the binary protocol used to exchange Wolfram Language expressions between a kernel and an external program. C programs use the WSTP library (`wstp.h`, built with `wsprep`/`mcc`); Java uses J/Link (`com.wolfram.jlink.KernelLink`); .NET uses .NET/Link. `LinkLaunch`, `LinkWrite`, `LinkRead` and `Install` drive links from inside Wolfram Language.

apis.name: Cloud deployment (CloudDeploy / APIFunction)
apis.description: `CloudDeploy` publishes a Wolfram Language object to a `CloudObject` URL. Wrapping the code in `APIFunction` produces a JSON/HTTP endpoint whose parameters are parsed by `Interpreter` types; `FormFunction` produces an interactive web form; `Delayed` produces a page recomputed on each request. `Permissions -> "Public"` makes the endpoint callable without authentication.
apis.example:
api = CloudDeploy[
   APIFunction[{"n" -> "Integer"}, Prime[#n] &, "JSON"],
   "nthprime", Permissions -> "Public"];
URLExecute[api, {"n" -> 1000}]

apis.name: ExternalEvaluate (calling out to other languages)
apis.description: Runs code in an external interpreter session from inside Wolfram Language and converts the result back into a Wolfram expression. Supported systems include `"Python"`, `"NodeJS"`, `"Shell"`, `"Julia"`, `"R"` and `"SQL"`. `StartExternalSession` keeps a persistent session, and `ExternalFunction` wraps an external function as a Wolfram Language function.

apis.name: Free-form and natural language input
apis.description: `WolframAlpha["query"]` sends natural language to Wolfram|Alpha and returns pods or a Wolfram Language expression; `Interpreter["type"]["text"]` parses a string into a typed entity, quantity or date; `SemanticImport` reads a data file and infers column types as quantities, dates and entities. Useful for turning user text into computable values inside an automated pipeline.
apis.example:
WolframAlpha["distance from earth to mars", "Result"]
Interpreter["Quantity"]["3 kilometers per second"]
Interpreter["Date"]["next friday"]

file_formats.description: Mathematica notebook: the interactive document format holding input and output cells, text, formatting, graphics and interactive interfaces. Itself a Wolfram Language expression (`Notebook[{Cell[...], ...}]`), so it can be generated and edited programmatically with `NotebookPut`, `NotebookWrite` and `Export`.

Wolfram Language package/source file (the modern replacement for `.m`). Plain UTF-8 text loaded with `Get["file.wl"]` or `Needs["Context`"]`; typically wrapped in `BeginPackage`/`EndPackage` to control which symbols are exported.

Wolfram Language script. Run with `wolframscript -script file.wls` or, on Unix, directly via a `#!/usr/bin/env wolframscript` shebang. Command-line arguments appear in `$ScriptCommandLine` and `Exit[n]` sets the process exit code.
Classic Mathematica package/source file, still fully supported and identical in content to `.wl`. Also the extension of the init files loaded from `$UserBaseDirectory/Kernel/init.m`.

Serialized Wolfram Language definitions in a platform- and version-specific binary format, written with `DumpSave` and loaded with `Get`. Loads far faster than re-parsing source, at the cost of portability between kernel versions.

Wolfram Exchange Format: a versioned, language-neutral binary serialization of arbitrary Wolfram Language expressions. The preferred interchange format between a kernel and external programs (the Python client library reads and writes it natively) via `Export[f, expr, "WXF"]` and `Import[f, "WXF"]`.
Serialized neural network from the Wolfram Neural Net framework, written with `Export["net.wlnet", net]` and read back with `Import`. Stores the layer graph together with learned arrays.

Computable Document Format: a notebook packaged so that its interactive `Manipulate` interfaces run in the free Wolfram Player. Produced with `CDFDeploy` or `Export["file.cdf", nb]` for distributing interactive documents to people without a Mathematica licence.
Wolfram Notebook Player/packaged notebook file used to distribute notebooks with restricted editing.
Paclet archive: the standard packaging and distribution unit for Wolfram Language libraries, installed with `PacletInstall` and discovered with `PacletFind`.
